title: 30 FPS vs 40 FPS on OLED: Retinal Judder, 120Hz Math & VRR Floor Guide
description: Engineering analysis of why sample-and-hold OLEDs exhibit stutter at 30 FPS, the mathematical perfection of 40 FPS in a 120Hz container, and HDMI 2.1 VRR 48Hz LFC behavior.
author: ToolkitGen Engineering Team
quickAnswer: 30 FPS appears choppier on modern OLEDs than older LCDs due to instantaneous pixel response times (<0.1 ms GtG) eliminating motion blur on sample-and-hold panels, causing static 33.3 ms frames to step jarringly across the retina. 40 FPS solves this on 120Hz displays through integer divider mathematics ($120 / 40 = 3$), providing a uniform 25.0 ms cadence that eliminates judder while saving 33% GPU rendering budget compared to 60 FPS. Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) below 48 Hz triggers Low Framerate Compensation (LFC), which can introduce near-black gamma flicker on OLED displays.
articleHtml:
Motion Perception & The Sample-and-Hold OLED Dilemma

Console gamers upgrading to state-of-the-art OLED televisions frequently report an unexpected visual paradox: high-budget 30 FPS console titles appear visibly choppier, harsher, and more stutter-prone than they did on ten-year-old LCD televisions. Far from being a defect, this phenomenon is the direct consequence of sample-and-hold display mechanics interacting with instantaneous pixel response times.

Display Timing & Frame Pacing Comparison

30 FPS in 60Hz Container

33.33 ms frame hold. $60 / 30 = 2$ refreshes per frame. Integer cadence, but severe sample-and-hold retinal stepping during lateral panning on OLEDs.

40 FPS in 60Hz Container

16.7 ms / 33.3 ms alternating hold. $60 / 40 = 1.5$ refreshes per frame. Fractional cadence creating violent rhythmic 3:2 motion judder.

40 FPS in 120Hz Container

25.00 ms uniform hold. $120 / 40 = 3$ refreshes per frame. Flawless 1:1:1 integer cadence eliminating judder with 33% lower GPU cost than 60 FPS.

1. The Physics of Sample-and-Hold: Retinal Stutter vs Motion Blur

To understand why 30 FPS appears jarring on modern panels, one must differentiate between pixel response time and display frame hold time:

  • Pixel Response Time (GtG): The time it takes for an individual display pixel to transition from one shade of gray to another. On modern OLED and QD-OLED panels, sub-millisecond response times are standard (typically 0.03 ms to 0.1 ms). On older twisted nematic (TN) or vertical alignment (VA) LCDs, response times ranged from 5 ms to 20 ms.
  • Display Frame Hold Time: The duration a rendered frame is held statically on screen before new pixel data is presented. At 30 FPS, frame hold time is exactly 33.33 milliseconds ($1000\text{ ms} / 30 = 33.33\text{ ms}$).

Human ocular tracking is continuous. When your eyes track a panning building or moving character, your retinas glide smoothly across the screen plane. However, on a sample-and-hold panel, the image does not move smoothly; it remains completely motionless for 33.33 milliseconds, then jumps instantaneously to the next coordinate.

On an older LCD, the sluggish 10 ms transition time acted as a natural spatial low-pass filter: as pixels slowly blended together, they generated physical motion blur that smoothed out the sharp positional jump. On an OLED, because pixels snap into place in 0.1 milliseconds, the image remains razor-sharp during its entire 33.33 ms static hold. When the eye tracks across this series of frozen, un-blurred frames, the brain perceives high-contrast positional jumps—a sensation known as retinal stutter or eye-tracking judder.

2. The Mathematical Elegance of 40 FPS in a 120Hz Container

For the first two years of the 9th console generation, players were forced to choose between 30 FPS Fidelity Modes and 60 FPS Performance Modes. However, 60 FPS requires cutting the per-frame render budget in half—from 33.3 ms down to 16.67 ms. On complex ray-traced engines, maintaining 60 FPS forced developers to drop internal rendering resolutions to 1080p or dynamic 1440p, disable ambient occlusion, and reduce crowd simulation density.

The introduction of HDMI 2.1 displays with native 120Hz refresh rates enabled a breakthrough: the 40 FPS Balanced Mode [Confirmed: Sony Interactive Entertainment, Insomniac Games].

The physics and mathematics of 40 FPS illustrate why this mode has become the gold standard for visual fidelity:

$$\text{Frame Budget (30 FPS)} = \frac{1000\text{ ms}}{30\text{ FPS}} = 33.33\text{ ms}$$
$$\text{Frame Budget (40 FPS)} = \frac{1000\text{ ms}}{40\text{ FPS}} = 25.00\text{ ms}\quad (-8.33\text{ ms} / 50\%\text{ of 60 FPS savings})$$
$$\text{Frame Budget (60 FPS)} = \frac{1000\text{ ms}}{60\text{ FPS}} = 16.67\text{ ms}\quad (-16.67\text{ ms})$$

Notice the non-linear relationship between frame rate and frame time. Moving from 30 FPS to 40 FPS gains 10 frames per second, but reclaims a massive 8.33 milliseconds of frame time—exactly half of the 16.67 ms gained by jumping all the way to 60 FPS! Yet, the GPU workload increases by only 33% ($40 / 30 = 1.33$), compared to the 100% compute increase required for 60 FPS.

Furthermore, on a 120Hz display, 120 divided by 40 equals an exact integer: $120 / 40 = 3.00$. The display scans each rendered frame precisely three times for 8.33 ms each, maintaining an unyielding 1:1:1 symmetric cadence. The frame hold time drops from 33.3 ms down to 25.0 ms, crossing the physiological perceptual threshold where retinal stutter substantially diminishes.

3. Why 40 FPS Cannot Run on a Standard 60Hz Screen

Attempting to run a 40 FPS title on a standard 60Hz television produces an unacceptable visual experience:

$$\text{Divider (60Hz / 40 FPS)} = 1.5\text{ Refreshes per Frame}$$

Because a display raster cannot present half a refresh, the timing controller must alternate: Frame 1 is shown for 1 refresh (16.67 ms), Frame 2 is shown for 2 refreshes (33.33 ms), Frame 3 is shown for 1 refresh (16.67 ms), and so forth. This asymmetric 1:2 repeat cadence induces jarring rhythmic judder that is significantly more irritating to the human visual cortex than a stable, locked 30 FPS feed.

4. HDMI 2.1 VRR Hardware Floor & Low Framerate Compensation (LFC)

Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) synchronizes display refresh timing to GPU rendering, allowing dynamic framerates without visual tearing. However, physical display timing controllers (TCONs) possess operational frequency floors. In the HDMI 2.1 and VESA Adaptive-Sync specifications, the native VRR window operates between 48 Hz and 120 Hz.

When a console title runs at 30 FPS or drops below 48 FPS, it falls outside the native VRR hardware boundary. To keep the display synchronized, the console GPU engages Low Framerate Compensation (LFC):

  • Frame Doubling: When a game renders at 30 FPS, the GPU presents each frame twice, driving the display panel at 60 Hz.
  • Frame Tripling: If frame delivery drops to 24 FPS, the GPU multiplies by 3x to drive the panel at 72 Hz.

5. The OLED Near-Black Gamma Flicker Phenomenon

While LFC maintains tear-free presentation, it introduces a well-documented optical side effect on self-emissive OLED panels: near-black gamma flickering [Confirmed: RTINGS, Blur Busters].

OLED sub-pixels are driven by micro-currents modulated by complex non-linear gamma lookup tables (LUTs). Because OLED thin-film transistors (TFTs) discharge slightly during the frame hold period, display manufacturers calibrate panel voltage curves specifically for a fixed refresh rate (typically 120Hz). When VRR dynamically modulates panel refresh between 48Hz and 120Hz—or rapidly bounces between native 48Hz and doubled 96Hz LFC states—the effective charging time of the pixel capacitors fluctuates.

In bright game scenes, this microscopic luminance variation is imperceptible. In dark, shadow-heavy scenes (such as caves, nighttime cityscapes, or horror environments), these rapid voltage shifts cause near-black luminance to pulse visibly, perceived as an annoying gray strobing or gamma flicker. To mitigate this on OLED panels, players can disable VRR for titles with locked 30 FPS framerates or utilize television-specific VRR fine-tuning adjustments (such as LG's 'Fine Tune Dark Areas' slider).

faq.q: Why does motion blur in game settings help with 30 FPS on OLED?
faq.a: Because OLED pixels have near-instant response times with zero native transition blur, turning on in-game camera motion blur artificially introduces directional blurring between frames, softening the positional steps across your retina and reducing perceived judder.

faq.q: Can I use 40 FPS mode on a 144Hz PC gaming monitor?
faq.a: 144 divided by 40 is 3.6, which is not an integer divider. However, if your 144Hz monitor supports FreeSync / G-Sync VRR, you can run 40 FPS smoothly with LFC frame doubling (driving the monitor at 80 Hz).

faq.q: Does 40 FPS increase controller input latency compared to 60 FPS?
faq.a: Yes. At 40 FPS, a frame is polled every 25.0 ms, compared to every 16.67 ms at 60 FPS. While input latency is slightly higher than 60 FPS, it represents a noticeable 8.33 ms responsiveness improvement over 30 FPS.

faq.q: Why do TV motion smoothing settings ruin gaming?
faq.a: Motion smoothing (MEMC / frame interpolation) requires buffering incoming frames in TV memory to generate artificial intermediate frames. This processing introduces 50 to 90 milliseconds of devastating input lag, making interactive gameplay feel disconnected and sluggish.
